glossary.SPECT: SPECT (Tomografía por emisión de fotón único)
glossary.BOLD: BOLD (dependiente del nivel de oxigenación sanguínea)

items.findings.infarct.title: Acute infarct, left MCA territory
items.findings.infarct.what: Brain tissue dying because the left middle cerebral artery is blocked.
items.findings.infarct.why: Cells lose energy within minutes, ion pumps fail and water moves into the cells (cytotoxic oedema). Water that can no longer diffuse freely lights up DWI first; free water (T2/FLAIR) and lower density (CT) follow over hours.
items.findings.clot.title: Clot in the left M1 segment
items.findings.clot.what: The thrombus blocking the middle cerebral artery.
items.findings.clot.why: Packed red cells are dense on CT (hyperdense MCA sign), dephase spins on SWI (susceptibility vessel sign) and stop flow-related signal on MRA, CTA and DSA.
items.findings.haem.title: Intracerebral haemorrhage
items.findings.haem.what: A bleed into the brain, here the classic hypertensive site in the putamen.
items.findings.haem.why: Fresh clot is dense on CT (protein and packed cells). On MR the signal depends on the iron state of haemoglobin, which changes over days: deoxyhaemoglobin (dark T2), methaemoglobin (bright T1), haemosiderin (dark rim).
items.findings.sah.title: Subarachnoid blood
items.findings.sah.what: Blood in the CSF spaces around the base of the brain.
items.findings.sah.why: Blood replaces dark CSF in the cisterns: dense on CT, and on FLAIR the protein-rich bloody CSF is no longer nulled so it turns bright.
items.findings.aneur_rupt.title: Ruptured ACom aneurysm
items.findings.aneur_rupt.what: Source of the haemorrhage: a sac on the anterior communicating artery.
items.findings.aneur_rupt.why: Seen on angiographic techniques as a contrast-filled outpouching.
items.findings.sdh.title: Acute subdural haematoma
items.findings.sdh.what: Torn bridging veins bleed into the space under the dura.
items.findings.sdh.why: Blood spreads freely under the dura, so it follows the curve of the brain as a crescent and can cross suture lines. It pushes the brain inward.
items.findings.edh.title: Epidural haematoma
items.findings.edh.what: Arterial bleed between skull and dura, usually the middle meningeal artery.
items.findings.edh.why: The dura is stuck to the skull at the sutures, so the blood bulges inward as a lens and stops at suture lines.
items.findings.fracture.title: Temporal bone fracture
items.findings.fracture.what: A linear crack in the thin squamous temporal bone.
items.findings.fracture.why: Bone is the brightest thing on CT; a fracture shows as a sharp dark line, best seen in the bone window.
items.findings.gbm.title: Glioblastoma
items.findings.gbm.what: The commonest and most aggressive primary brain tumour (WHO grade 4).
items.findings.gbm.why: Leaky new vessels let contrast into the rim; the centre outgrows its blood supply and dies (necrosis). Vasogenic oedema spreads along white-matter tracts but spares the cortex.
items.findings.met.title: Metastasis
items.findings.met.what: A deposit of cancer that has spread through the blood.
items.findings.met.why: Tumour cells lodge where vessels narrow at the grey–white junction. They have leaky vessels (enhance) and provoke a lot of vasogenic oedema.
items.findings.abscess.title: Pyogenic abscess
items.findings.abscess.what: A bacterial infection walled off by a capsule.
items.findings.abscess.why: Thick, viscous pus restricts water diffusion, so the core is bright on DWI and dark on ADC — the key difference from tumour necrosis. The capsule makes a thin, smooth enhancing ring.
items.findings.plaque.title: Demyelinating plaque
items.findings.plaque.what: An area where the myelin around axons has been stripped by inflammation.
items.findings.plaque.why: Loss of myelin frees water (bright on T2/FLAIR). Plaques form around small veins that run out from the ventricles, so they line up at right angles to them.
items.findings.active.title: Active (enhancing) plaque
items.findings.active.why: Inflammation opens the blood–brain barrier, so gadolinium leaks in, often as an open ring facing the cortex.
items.findings.hippo.title: Hippocampal atrophy
items.findings.hippo.what: Shrinkage of the memory centres in the medial temporal lobes.
items.findings.hippo.why: Neurofibrillary tangles and neuron loss start in the entorhinal cortex and hippocampus, so these shrink first and the temporal horns widen.
items.findings.tp.title: Temporoparietal hypometabolism
items.findings.tp.what: Reduced glucose use in posterior association cortex and posterior cingulate.
items.findings.tp.why: Synaptic failure lowers energy demand before tissue is lost, so PET shows the disease pattern years before atrophy is obvious.
items.findings.mts.title: Mesial temporal sclerosis
items.findings.mts.what: Neuron loss and scarring (gliosis) in the left hippocampus.
items.findings.mts.why: Scarring raises water content (bright T2/FLAIR) and lost neurons shrink the structure, so the temporal horn grows.
items.findings.tle_pet.title: Left temporal hypometabolism
items.findings.tle_pet.what: The epileptogenic temporal lobe uses less glucose between seizures.
items.findings.tle_pet.why: Interictal dysfunction and neuron loss lower metabolism around the focus, often more widely than the MRI lesion.
items.findings.tle_spect.title: Ictal hyperperfusion
items.findings.tle_spect.what: Blood flow surges in the seizure focus during the seizure.
items.findings.tle_spect.why: HMPAO is trapped within a minute of injection, freezing the blood-flow pattern of that moment for later scanning.
items.findings.hydro.title: Ventricular enlargement
items.findings.hydro.what: The lateral and third ventricles are dilated.
items.findings.hydro.why: CSF keeps being produced by the choroid plexus but cannot drain past the narrowed cerebral aqueduct, so pressure balloons the ventricles upstream.
items.findings.dat_loss.title: Reduced putamen uptake
items.findings.dat_loss.what: Loss of dopamine transporters in the left striatum.
items.findings.dat_loss.why: Nigrostriatal neurons die from the back of the putamen forward, so uptake fades posterior-first and on the side opposite the worse symptoms.
items.findings.aneur.title: Saccular aneurysm
items.findings.aneur.what: A berry-shaped outpouching at the left MCA bifurcation.
items.findings.aneur.why: Flow hits the apex of the branch point where the vessel wall media is weakest.
items.findings.avm.title: Arteriovenous malformation
items.findings.avm.what: Arteries connect straight to veins through a tangle (nidus) with no capillary bed.
items.findings.avm.why: High-flow vessels appear as flow voids on T2, and on angiography the veins fill early, at the same time as the arteries.
items.findings.nofill.title: Absent intracranial filling
items.findings.nofill.what: No contrast or tracer reaches the brain.
items.findings.nofill.why: When intracranial pressure exceeds arterial pressure, blood can no longer enter the skull.
items.findings.ivh.title: Germinal matrix haemorrhage
items.findings.ivh.what: Bleeding into the left lateral ventricle in a preterm infant.
items.findings.ivh.why: Fresh clot reflects sound strongly, so it is bright inside the normally echo-free ventricle.
items.findings.pvl.title: Periventricular flare
items.findings.pvl.what: Injured white matter beside the ventricles.
items.findings.pvl.why: Oedematous, injured white matter scatters more sound and looks brighter than the choroid plexus.
items.findings.uws.title: Posterior medial hypometabolism
items.findings.uws.what: Low metabolism in the precuneus and posterior cingulate.
items.findings.uws.why: These hubs are among the most active at rest in conscious people; their recovery tracks the return of awareness.
